Has the Project Development Objective been changed since Board Approval of the Project Objective? No Components Table Name Works under Part A of the Project:(Cost $267.80 M) Goods, consultantsâ services, Training and Operating Costs under Part B of the Project:(Cost $26.80 M) Price Contingency Goods, Works, consultantsâ services, Training and Operating Costs under Part C of the Project:(Cost $5.00 M) Resettlement Compensation under Part D of the Project:(Cost $4.80 M) Overall Ratings Name Previous Rating Current Rating Progress towards achievement of PDO Satisfactory Satisfactory Overall Implementation Progress (IP) Moderately Satisfactory Moderately Satisfactory Overall Risk Rating Substantial Substantial Implementation Status and Key Decisions Overall disbursement for all sources of funds stands for LIBRAMP at 96%, including 93% of IDA funds and 100% of LRTF funds (the LRTF Grant closed in June of 2021). Progress towards the achievement is rated satisfactory on the basis of the achievement of the PDO indicators, while the implementation progress is rated moderately satisfactory. Key achievements to date include the rehabilitation of the entire Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border road (Suakoko Highway). The rehabilitation of the rural section was completed in 2016 and is under the long-term maintenance phases under the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The urban section was substantially completed in May 2023.

The travel time along the road has reduced by 50% and the road remains in overall good physical condition, and the levels of service are largely achieved. The completion of this road has 6/14/2023 Page 1 of 7 The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) increased the stock of roads in good and fair condition from 33.7 to 34.5% of the classified paved road network. A Multi-Modal Transport Plan (including a Strategic Investment Plan) has been formulated and 915 RAP entitlements have also been fully paid with IDA funding under the project. Under Road Safety Component, the following has also been achieved (i) Road safety schoolbooks (125,000No.) printed, (ii) Streets Naming, Traffic Warning & County Welcome Signs installed, (iii) Training undertaken for truck drivers commercial and motorcycle and (iv) communications (toll free number 5888) for emergency response system for post-crash response operational; (v) Road marking completed for 15km out of 62km of streets in Monrovia; (vi) speed guns and breathalyzers procured for Liberia National Police (LNP) and training in various aspects of road safety carried out for a total of 1,109 staff across agencies, including 693 women (62%). The government has communicated its decision on the counterpart funding for the OPRC Lots 1 and 2, essentially rescheduling its counterpart funding contribution to the project over the next three budget years.

The project is currently being restructured to reflect this change in the funding arrangements. The Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border road (Suakoko Highway) whose rehabilitation was completed in 2016 is under a long-term maintenance phase of the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The implementation of the rehabilitation of the urban section of the project corridor from SC Cooper to ELWA Junction to Red Light to Coca Cola Factory commenced in January 2019 with the first 2.1km length between Red Light and Coca Cola Junction completed in March 2020. An extension of the rehabilitation completion date by about 23 months will be required to complete the works. The road sector reform agenda has made little progress with the draft the Road Act and Road Agency Act stalled. Government action is needed on this, and on the strengthening of the NRF which continues to receive irregular and inadequate transfers of collected fuel levies, which undermines the overall objective of road maintenance.

The project is on course to achieve all its targets and indicators. The additional financing (US$40 million) approved in May 2017 was declared effective January 24, 2018. Suakoko Highway is under a long term maintenance phase of the two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs). The road, which extends from Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border, remains in overall good physical condition. The road sector reform has slowed recently.

However, some progress is made regarding the road fund. A road fund manager is appointed and the Government is in the process of setting up road fund accounts. There is a legal challenge against collection of fuel levy by the road fund. The Supreme Court has stayed the collection of road fund levy following the legal challenge. The issue is yet to be resolved. However, the Supreme Court decision is expected in June 2018. The Highway Act and Road Agency Act are prepared. They are expected to be taken up by the new Legislature soon. The implementation of the rehabilitation of the ELWA Junction to Red Light Road section (6.5km), planned to commence by March 2018, is delayed. The project is on course to achieve all its targets and indicators. Currently there are no major issues linked to the project. The World Bank Board of Directors has approved an additional financing ($40 million) to the existing project has been approved in May 2017. An agreement between the World Bank and the Government has already been signed.

However, the additional financing is yet to be made effective, as Parliament is yet to concur with the agreement, and comments from the Ministry of Justice are yet to be received. It is expected that the project will be effective by end-January, 2018, after completion of all formalities. Two 10-year Output and Performance Based Contracts (OPRCs) along the Monrovia–Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea Border Road have successfully entered their maintenance phases, after completion of the rehabilitation works for two contracts between September, 2017 and March, 2017, apart from a few instances. Monitoring Consultants are working diligently to facilitate the contract supervision. The road sector reform has been progressing well, albeit the process has been observed to be slow. The Parliament has approved the Road Fund Act in December, 2016, which was made effective from July 1, 2017. However, it is yet to be made operational. The Bank Task Team has been working closely with the Government to make the fund operational. The Road Act has been drafted and consulted. However, the Road Agency Act has been facing issues. One of the main issues being faced is the legal aspects of roles and responsibilities between the proposed Road Agency and the Ministry of Public Works. It now appears that these two pieces of legislation might be placed before the new Parliament; voting for selection of the legislators was only held in October 10, 2017.

The implementation of the rehabilitation of the ELWA Junction to Red Light Road section (6.5km) is planned to commence by March 2018 after the completion of prior activities including the selection of contractors and the implementation of the Resettlement Action Plan. Rehabilitation of the LIBRAMP corridor (248 km) is completed, a dedication ceremony was held in October 2016, and the road has been renamed Suakoko Highway. Lot 1 (178 km) entered the maintenance phase in September 2016, while Lot 2 did so in March. Despite physical progress, cost overruns and exchange rate losses mean LIBRAMP will require additional financial resources. The government has also been unable to contribute the promised counterpart financing (US$72.8 million over ten years). The government is considering various options to mitigate the situation and project risk, such as requesting additional financing or dropping some pending activities, and a response is pending.

A public employee has admitted responsibility for theft of five missing RAP payments checks. Restitution has been received for one check, leaving an ineligible expenditure balance of US$11,348. Unless further restitution is paid, the World Bank will request the ineligible expenditure be returned by the Government of Liberia (GoL). Residents in some areas have raised concern about impacts of road construction equipment vibration on their homes. The IIU has been asked to ensure an appropriate and accessible project Grievance Redress Mechanism is triggered to follow up on all claims of property damage under the project. As mentioned in the previous ISR sequence, the improvement in pavement condition has led to increased traffic speeds and had a negative impact on road safety in the short term. A partial road safety assessment had identified national-level and corridor-level road safety deficiencies The Monitoring Consultant for Lots 1 has been tasked to submit report on road safety along the corridor by end November 2016. The Infrastructure Implementation Unit of the Ministry of Public Works and the Government have yet to resolve outstanding contractual issues. Variation orders to account for Ebola-related force majeure and delayed site handover are yet to be finalized for the Lot 1 works contract. Refund of previously levied import taxes (due to change in regulations) is still pending US$1.3 million.

The government has agreed to clarify procedures for this reimbursement process but has so far not done so. The Lot 1 Contractor is owed an additional US$490,000 for explosive import costs due to new government regulations. The services for preparing the concept design and bidding documents for ELWA Junction-Red Light intersection -Coca Cola Factory road section are ongoing. Consultants have also been fully mobilized since May 2015. The payments to remaining Project Affected Persons (PAPs) was completed by June 2015 and the site handover has since been completed. Significant progress has been achieved over the period with about 75% of the entire road bituminous surfaced. On the other hand, the improvements in the riding quality has impacted negatively on road safety in the short term, resulting from a combination of factors low vehicle quality and inadequate driver skills.

The project authorities are planning to carry out sensitization of the communities living within the road corridor and road users on road safety is planned. There are a few critical issues that need to be resolved quickly to maintain the momentum of implementation. Variation orders need to be finalized for works contracts in light of the Ebola delays and revised handover schedule. The cost increases are yet to be finalized and agreed; early estimates indicate that it could be substantial. Duty free import of fuel has been streamlined but refund of previously levied import taxes (due to change in regulations) is still pending. IIU will finalize the terms of reference for the Multimodal Transport Plan and Strategic Investment Plan by the fourth quarter of 2015. The procurement for preparing the concept design and bidding documents for ELWA Junction-Red Light intersection -Coca Cola Factory road section is in progress the consultant is likely to be hired by October, 2015.

v The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT I. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL 1. At project appraisal, Liberia was one of Africa’s poorest countries with a gross domestic product (GDP) per capita of US$210 in 2009. The country managed to sustain its growth amidst these challenges with a GDP growth of 9.7 percent in 2007, 7.1 percent in 2008, and 4.9 percent (estimated) in 2009.2 Liberia’s economic growth slowed down in 2009 due to low commodity prices resulting from the global economic downturn. Infrastructural loses from the 14-year civil war presented serious challenges to economic development despite the post-war political stability in Liberia. Extensive destruction of basic infrastructure, absence of maintenance, poor education and health indicators, limited transportation and communications connectivity, ethnic loyalties, and weak public institutions limited the use of natural wealth and citizenry cohesion to promote sustainable and broad-based income growth.3 Most of the 10,000 km of existing roads were in extreme disrepair and non-motorable during the rainy seasons and were, therefore, identified as a priority need for development and infrastructural rehabilitation during the development of the Poverty Reduction Strategy (PRS). 2.

In 2008, through the National Transport Policy and Strategy initiated by the World Bank and supported by the German Technical Cooperation (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit, GTZ), medium- and long-term goals were set to revamp the road sector. The goals focused on contracting arrangement, maintenance strategy, and institutional formulation. A self-standing Infrastructure Implementation Unit (IIU) with greater decision-making authority was established out of this strategy in 2009. The IIU was a transformation of the Special Implementation Unit which was set up in 2006 under the Ministry of Public Works (MPW) to be the implementation unit for IDA and other donor-funded infrastructure projects with the broader aim of improving capacity in the road sector. 3. To direct Liberia’s reformation agenda, a Country Assistance Strategy (CAS) was also prepared in 2009 through joint funding from IDA, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and the African Development Bank (AfDB). The CAS was designed to respond to core strategic areas mostly affected by the civil war, which included intervention on peace and security, economic revitalization, strengthening of governance and rule of law, and infrastructure and basic services provided in the PRS in 2008. The CAS had three strategic themes: (a) rebuilding core state functions and institutions; (b) rehabilitating infrastructure to jump-start economic growth; and (c) facilitating pro-poor growth.

Infrastructure rehabilitation and long-term management and preservation of assets were identified as major prerequisites for attainment of the long-term CAS outcomes of improving services, economy, and social conditions. 4. The Liberia Road Asset Management Project (LIBRAMP) became a key part of the CAS due to road maintenance and funding needs of the government. The project’s aim was not to only reconstruct damaged roads but also to enhance connectivity between urban and rural areas as well as between Liberia and its neighboring countries to expand trade and provide access to services and jobs to catalyze Liberia’s growth and sustainable development in the road sector. For this purpose, the Monrovia-Guinea border road corridor was chosen for the project. The corridor is important and was core to the nation’s reconstruction as it connects the five largest cities in Liberia and provides cross-border connections. For the long-term preservation of the road asset, the project preparation recognized the need for adequate financing for routine maintenance (RM) and periodic maintenance (PM) through annual budgets and anticipated donor support for maintenance as well. The project preparation also envisaged further improvement in the road network condition and was hence designed to discuss a more reliable and bigger funding for road maintenance through the establishment of a road fund.

The project was hence endorsed with funding support from international donors which was coordinated by the 2Project Appraisal Document (2011) 3World Bank, 2018. LIBRAMP was in a position to receive financing from the World Bank as well since Liberia had become IDA creditworthy post recovery and progress in implementing the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) reform in June 2010 including the Public Financial Management Law. 5. LIBRAMP design benefited from lessons from existing projects, mostly those on output-based contracts. The output-based contract was the first in Liberia and the sub-region. A long term (ten-year) output and performance-based road contract (OPRC) approach which required commitment from all parties was opted for the design of LIBRAMP to provide both rehabilitation and maintenance on the Monrovia-Guinea border road corridor. The long-term OPRC was to provide the road network in Liberia with a consistent and appropriate level of service over the medium term instead of using a series of traditional contracts. The method aimed to ensure institutional development over the long term while safeguarding the road lifespan with an efficient maintenance mechanism. Project Development Objectives (PDOs) 6.

The PDO as defined in the PAD and financing agreement was to “support the Recipient’s efforts to reduce transport costs along the road corridor from Monrovia to the Guinea border and to maintain the road in good condition over a ten-year period” and remained unchanged until project completion. RELEVANCE OF PDO Assessment of Relevance of PDOs and Rating 15. The project activities were well-aligned with Liberia’s National Development Plans (NDPs). Specifically, the project was aligned with the Pro-Poor Agenda for Prosperity and Development (PAPD) for 2018 to 2023 which is the second in the series of the five-year NDPs.5 The PAPD outlined a development outcome that sought to increase economic activity and connectivity through critical roads under its Pillar 2—economy and jobs. The specific road corridor connects the urban areas within Nimda County to the rural areas and the neighboring country, Guinea, and provides access to jobs and services among counties and between the rural and urban areas.

The Monrovia-Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea border road corridor is the country’s backbone and connects places along the corridor to the capital, Monrovia, as well as to Guinea and Sierra Leone. The road is part of the Core Roads for Economic Growth and Transformation (CREAT)6 created to connect areas with high developmental potential with the far-flung less developed areas. The road corridor has a high potential to bring socioeconomic development to Liberia. 16. The PDO remained consistent with the current World Bank Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for Liberia for the period FY19 to FY24.7 The PDO is specifically aligned to Pillar 3 of the CPF which looks at “narrowing the infrastructure gap to foster more equitable development nationwide” and more particularly addresses Objective 7 which aims at 5 https://globalnaps.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/liberia-national-development-agenda-pro-poor-agenda.pdf 6 The total length of CREAT is 3,322 km and includes already implemented paved roads (700.46 km) to be maintained under potential long-term OPRC or PBMC methods. 7 https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/374031541438293964/pdf/liberia-cpf-11012018-636768792698663889.pdf Page 5 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT “improved access to utilities, markets, and community services.” The PDO’s relevance is further emphasized in the priority policy areas and development interventions in the Systematic Country Diagnostic (SCD) for FY20.

The project objective is covered adequately under Policy Area A which aims at enhancing productivity-driven growth, diversification, and job creation. Specifically, the project supplements government efforts to close the road infrastructure gap which this policy statement aims at. In addition, the road corridor, which is the main linkage between Monrovia and Guinea, will enhance trade among the two countries and strengthen regional cooperation and coordination to address Policy Area 4 - Prudent Economic Management and Building Resilience to Shocks. 17. Considering the above, the relevance of the PDO is rated High. B. ACHIEVEMENT OF PDOs (EFFICACY) Assessment of Achievement of Each Objective/Outcome 18. The Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) rated the overall PDO based on the achievement of the individual project outcome/objectives at project close as discussed below. PDO 1: Reduce transport costs along the road corridor from Monrovia 19. Achievement of PDO 1 is rated Substantial since it was achieved and the road remains in a good condition to benefit users in term of reduction in transport-related cost. 20. The project achieved its target outcomes. Prior to the project interventions, the surface of the road corridor was in very poor condition with a mix of surface types including asphalt concrete from Monrovia to Gbarnga, a deteriorated asphalt surface treatment from Gbarnga to Ganta, and a gravel surfaced road between Ganta and the Guinea border (2 km).

The project financed the rehabilitation, including sections of new construction and annual RM of the corridor through the OPRC, which improved the road surface and riding condition for both urban and rural sections. The road’s IRI, which measures the ride quality, improved from 12 percent to less than 3 percent after the rehabilitation. The last IRI was measured in November 2024, after the project had closed, and recorded an average IRI of 2.19 percent, lesser than the 3 percent target set for June 2024. An actual vehicle operation cost (VOC) and delay reduction measurement would have been more useful. Notwithstanding, the IRI is considered a proxy indicator for VOC and delay levels, therefore, the low IRI recorded four months after project close is indicative of better riding quality which potentially will result in reduced VOC, travel delays, and transport costs. A road user survey was also undertaken to determine user satisfaction regarding the improved road before project closing. Out of the 1,000 respondents, 62 percent indicated that their travel time has reduced and were satisfied with the road improvement. 21. The improved road and intersection in Monrovia directly benefited 362,905 people in the rural areas as anticipated and people in the urban area in Monrovia. The benefits were in various forms from reduction in travel time and increased access to jobs and services as noted from the survey, and potentially a reduction in VOC, among other expected benefits.

Almost two thirds (63 percent) of the survey participants indicated that the road has made it convenient for them to access their homes and basic amenities like school, work, market, and hospital. With the improvement in connectivity and accessibility, a boost in the national economy is expected through increased intercity trade among the corridor cities8, counties, and regional trade and commerce with neighboring countries like Guinea. 8 This road connects four of the country’s five largest cities: Monrovia, Ganta, Buchanan, Kakata, and Gbarnga. Page 6 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT PDO-2: Maintain the road in good condition over a 10-year period 22. PDO -2 is rated Substantial based on the below assessment. 23. The entire 253 km road from ELWA intersection in Monrovia to the Guinea border remains in good condition. The rehabilitated and constructed road has increased the stock of roads in good and fair condition from 1 percent to 34.5 percent out of the 746 km classified paved roads. RM works which included vegetation control, desilting, and cleaning of drainage facilities has preserved the life of the road from early deterioration. The RM which was expected to be implemented throughout the ten-year contract period was started after rehabilitation works in 2016 and suspended in 2022 due to lack of payment by the GOL.

The PM work, which initially included an asphalt overlay in year 8–9 for the entire 249 km road, was not undertaken despites the revision of the overlay length to about 50km based on the good condition reflected in the pavement assessment.9 All outstanding maintenance works will be funded after LIBRAMP closure by the government per agreement with the contracting entity (CE) under Variation Order (VO) 4 and 1 for Lot 2 and 1 respectively. The RM was expected to start in June 2024 and has not whilst the PM will commence in March 2025 for Lot 1 and Lot 2 (see tables 7.3 and 7.5 in annex 7). Despite the maintenance activity lapses, the road continues to be in good state physically and provides all year-round access to 362,905 rural people who make up about 11% of the rural population in Liberia. 24. A ten-year Multimodal Transport Development Plan and five-year Strategic Plan for 2022 to 2027 were developed under the project. The two plans documented the transport sector’s institutional, infrastructural, and regulatory short-, medium-, and long-term needs and accompanying resource requirements. The strategic plan, endorsed by the sector institutions, outlines a timely maintenance plan before and after the project closure under thematic area 1—to provide quality and efficient Infrastructure.

This plan formed the basis for the Road Sector Development Plan (RSDP).10 The project further supported the formation of the National Road Fund (NRF) by driving the enactment and operationalization of the Road Fund Act (2016) and capacity strengthening to ensure the sustenance of dedicated funds for road maintenance in Liberia. Currently, fuel levy remains the only source of funds for the NRF despite other named sources like user charges and tolls. Per the NRF quarterly financial statements, in June 2024, US$4,788,152.22 out of the US$7,633,671.85 fuel levy collected was remitted by the Ministry of Finance to the NRF escrow accounts for road maintenance-related works which is inadequate for the sector. The NRF is undertaking road user charges studies and technical assessments to identify additional fund sources and to limit operational inefficiencies in the sector. 25. The road sector institutions’ capacity to manage road assets has improved. The IIU, for the past 13 years, has seen growth in staff numbers and quality through on-the-job and off-site training facilitated by international consultants, experts, and the World Bank to efficiently undertake contract management and administration. Currently, all positions under the 4 key competence areas in the IIU: a) planning and budgeting; (b) financial management; (c) procurement and contract management; and (d) monitoring and evaluation, have been filled by qualified staff who were limited and comprised 10 percent in 2011.

Knowledge and skills were transferred to the IIU and the Public Financial Management Unit (PFMU, the adjunct finance staff) through extensive on-the-job-training through the monitoring consultants (MCs), training seminars and workshops. Experiences gained in managing the multi-donor, complex, and long-duration OPRCs puts the IIU in a better position to support the road sector improvement and constitute a workforce which can initiate a robust road authority. The capacity of the IIU has significantly improved over the last 13 years. The IIU has progressively filled all the four key competence areas with qualified staff who only made up 10% of the total staff in 2011 during the project appraisal.

The four key areas are in: (a) planning and budgeting; (b) financial management; (c) procurement and contract management; and (d) monitoring and evaluation. The achievement is indicative of improved local capacity in the sector. A performance evaluation framework developed with the help of the World Bank is being used to monitor yearly staff performance to ensure productivity and efficiency at the IIU. Capacity-building activities were tailored to enhance Page 10 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT the IIU in anticipation of the establishment of the road agency or authority from the IIU to be responsible for all aspects of the road sector.12 36. The improved riding quality of the road led to increased speeds and subsequent road crash increment which was not anticipated. A road safety action plan was therefore produced and implemented partly to curtail the impact. III. KEY FACTORS AFFECTED IMPLEMENTATION AND OUTCOME A. KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION 42. The project was designed to efficiently restore the destroyed road infrastructure and low institutional capacity in Liberia’s road sector after the war. With the deplorable road condition and economic challenges in Liberia, the traditional input-based road maintenance contract which required three different contracts for rehabilitation, RM, and PM works was deemed a more expensive, less efficient, and less attractive option.

Adopting an OPRC with longer duration and a single entity for all three works presented a better choice for accountability and efficiency and a good avenue for long-term capacity building for the road sector. Per the countries condition at the time, the 10 years OPRC was a more attractive option for private sector participation in the form of CEs. 43. The project was structured on lessons learned from OPRC projects worldwide. Liberia is the first in the sub- region to undertake an OPRC and the project design benefited from the lessons learnt from ongoing or completed OPRCs in some countries.14 The lessons highlighted potential risk, payment model for both rehabilitation and maintenance works, long term network management interventions to spread the contractor’s risk, and World Bank inclusion throughout the project life. The project leveraged the World Bank’s convening power and technical expertise on OPRCs and in coordinating development partners through LTDF administration. B. KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION 44. The project was expected to be implemented in ten years to include three years of rehabilitation and seven years of maintenance but took 13 years. At project close, the RM had not been fully implemented and the revised PM had not been started. The challenges and successes during implementation were attributable to the factors discussed below. a. Factors subject to government control 45.

Key among the implementation challenges was the inability of the GOL to provide its overall funding contribution of US$47.8 million. Liberia faced numerous macroeconomic constraints which led to an International Monetary Fund (IMF) program in 2019 and the GOL’s failure to contribute to finance claims and RM and PM activities under Component 1 as well as RAP implementation.15 The RM was suspended on October 1, 2022, and the asphalt overlay activity under the PM was never started. The GOL’s failure to finance RAP implementation delayed site handover to the CE and rehabilitation works by close to 17 months. Sites were fully handed over to the CE at the end of July 2015, after work commencement in 2012 and 2013 for Lot 1 and 2, respectively. While US$10 million IDA funds under the Urban and Rural Infrastructure Rehabilitation Project (URIRP) financed RAP compensation payments for Lot 1 and Lot 2, US$5 million under LIBRAMP AF2 was sourced for the urban road section. 14 Countries in Latin America (Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay), South Asia (India), and Africa (Chad, Zambia, and Botswana) were identified with OPRC experience at appraisal. 15 RAP compensation for Lots 1 and 2 was provided from IDA resources under the URIRP (P113099) while for the 6.1 km urban road it was from IDA resources under AF2 of LIBRAMP. Aside from the RAP implementation, the country’s regulations changes and contractual noncompliance issues also delayed the project. New regulation from the Ministry of Lands, Mines, and Energy to restrict importation of explosives to a single entity with limited capacity disrupted the activities of the CEs, leading to delays and uncertainty regarding quarrying activities. The reversal of the tax exemption agreement on fuel imports by the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) contributed to the cost overrun from claims and the delay in payment thereof also resulted in accrued interests on the tax levies collected from the CE. 47. Contract administration lapses and delay in decision-making by the IIU led to claims with associated interests. Late and lack of reporting on pertinent issue like the theft of five cancelled cheques16 for RAP compensation and other noncompliance issues by the IIU was observed. The government through the project’s private bank, Liberian Bank for Development and Investment (LBDI), has recouped, as of 2017, all the stolen cheques which were categorized as ineligible expenses. The procurement team of the IIU on the other hand showed in-depth experience in handling IDA and other donor-funded projects and their familiarity with World Bank guidelines and procedures was found useful for project delivery. 48. Low oversight and compliance enforcement by the GOL and the IIU on environmental and social (E&S) issues slowed project progress and performance.

Incidences of E&S noncompliance led to suspension, downgrading of implementation performance, and additional cost implications. The largest was the forceful eviction of the 3,227 registered and unregistered petty traders by the GOL on July 12, 2021, to give RoW to the CE at the Redlight intersection of the 6.1 km urban road section. The lack of compliance of the CE with the Environmental Management Plan (EMP) and Health, Safety, and Environmental Management Plan (HSEMP) implementation particularly on restoration of quarry sites was also a key environmental issue. For noncompliance with the EMP and contractor’s HSEMP, there were no explicit penalties imposed on the CE, leaving the MC with limited means to manage non-conformance. The investigation and preparation of a remedial action plan for the OP4.12 noncompliance regarding the petty traders led to about 18 months of delay to the project. The action plan included compensation for the petty traders for income loss and property damage to the petty traders over the 180-day eviction period. 49. In view of the GOL’s inability to fund the petty traders’ compensation, IDA financing of US$2.15 million under the Rural Economic Transformation Project (RETRAP) AF2 17 has been arranged.

Beside the challenge of the IIU and Grievance Redress Committee (GRC) in locating the unregistered transient traders, the implementation of the compensation could not be completed at the project closing due to a RETRAP Legal Agreement covenant.18 All E&S issues which could not be completed during the project tenure are captured in the action plan in table 7.1 in annex 7. b. Factors outside the control of the government, IIU, and World Bank 50. The project experienced two major disease outbreaks during its implementation: the Ebola virus in 2014 and the SARS COV-2 (COVID-19) in 2020. Even though the EVD outbreak was covered under force majeure contractually, the death of four project staff in the Lot 2 campsite led to the site closing and halting of activities from August 2014 for about seven months. The COVID-19 pandemic slowed down work on the 6.1 km urban section from March 2020, delaying the urban site handover till December 2020, and led to the termination of the contract of the Lot 1 MC which was taken over by the MC for Lot 2. 16 The PFMU cancelled 21 ‘returned’ cheques totaling US$118,796 out of which five worth US$16,748 were stolen. 17 The IDA funding of AF2 to the RETRAP(P181083) financed the entire petty traders’ compensation under a contingency arrangement approved by the Regional Vice President (RVP).

The compensation was part of the action plan to correct the OP4.12 noncompliance involving 1,653 semi-mobile petty traders and 1,574 fully transient petty traders who were forcefully evicted from the urban section from June 2021 to February 2022. 18 The compensation of US$180,000 for the registered petty traders is to be released under a contingency category after the RVP and restructuring. QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E) M&E Design 52. The PDO achievement and progress were designed to be measured by output and outcome indicators.

The indicators measured two thematic areas: (a) road network development and performance which measured the improvement in physical road network condition and benefit in transport cost to road users and (b) institutional development which measured the progress and results of capacity-building interventions under intermediate indicators. The project control team/IIU were assigned the responsibility of the daily project management and overall monitoring and reporting on the RF at appraisal while the MCs assisted the IIU by regular monitoring of compliance and service-level criteria of the road. M&E TA and training was provided under Component 2. 53. The RF was clearly defined. Baseline and target values as well as methodology, data source, and frequency of data collection were defined at appraisal and revised where necessary under the various restructurings. The methodologies for each indicator were succinct; however, for an indicator like the transport cost borne by road users, actual VOC and travel time measurements would have been more appropriate compared to the use of IRI which is a proxy. Also, the indicator to measure maintenance, ‘roads maintained’, was not succinct as it failed to differentiate PM from RM and did not account for a time-bound result as was the design. M&E Implementation 54. The RF was revised through three of the four restructurings.

At the close of the project, the RF consisted of four PDO indicators and twelve intermediate indicators from the appraisal’s four PDO and six intermediate indicators. The changes in indicators, outlined in table 2 were due to (a) removal or reduction of certain activities due to lack of counterpart financing, leading to the dropping of some indicators and (b) scale-up of component and activities to support road safety and enhance connectivity between urban and rural areas. Data collection for the PDO indicators was robustly done till June 2022, when data collection and monitoring was halted due to project suspension. The PDO indicators were not measured from 2022 till project close. 55. The IIU did not hire or designate an M&E specialist to oversee the RF data collection, review, and evaluation. While the IRI and Component 1 intermediate indicators were collected by the CE under the supervision of the MC, the other PDO and intermediate indicators were to be collected and reported by the IIU. Collection, collation, dissemination, and monitoring of the data from the various entities was poorly done resulting in inconsistency in reporting on values and updating of indicators between the World Bank and the client.

Some indicators like ‘hired female staff in the IIU’ and ‘percentage of citizen complaints addressed within seven days’, which was to monitor the performance of the grievance Page 14 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT redress mechanism under the Argo app,19 were never reported, even though data was measured. Others like IRI were not keenly monitored and measured as designed. The mid-term review report by the MC recommended a person within the IIU to be designated as the M&E lead officer, which was not addressed. 56. The economic and social indicator recommended during appraisal to support future investment decision- making was not undertaken. The indicator was to measure travel pattern information, agriculture prices, transport cost as a share of household income, access to health and education facilities, and other accessibility and mobility related information. These indicators which were not part of the RF was intended for future planning and a broad assessment of the investment impact. A road user satisfaction survey was undertaken in place of the social and economic studies. The survey was however carried out eight years after rehabilitation was completed and may record under- or over-estimated views of respondents due to the long recall period. M&E Utilization 57. The PDO and intermediate indicators were useful in monitoring project progress and ensuring compliance to quality.

The progress on indicators was instrumental in the overall decision-making of key players for additional financing, extension of the closing date, and payment to the CE. The capacity-building indicator under Component 2 is expected to improve the preparedness of the IIU toward their reformation into a road authority. The project’s M&E framework was well-designed; however, it would have benefitted more from inclusion of the social/economic indicators and actual measurements of VOCs to inform other future investments’ decision-making. The IIU was responsible for the procurement and hired two procurement specialists as stipulated in the legal covenants. The project procurement risk and performance were Substantial and Moderately Satisfactory, respectively, at closure. The procurement implementation status recorded positive progress. A total of 30 contracts planned were awarded and completed. In the procurement process, the project used appropriate market approaches and considerations were given to size, value, and complexity of the procurement package, and all were consistent with the legal framework. Clear procurement documents, proportionate to the need, were used to encourage broad participation from potential competitors. IDA procurement procedures have been well followed, both through open market and national markets methods. The Agency effectively managed contracts to ensure delivery per the contract conditions. The selection and award processes were carried out effectively, efficiently, and transparently. Contracts and payment documents were uploaded in the Systematic Tracking of Exchanges in Procurement (STEP) system promptly, except for a few activities that the project finally uploaded during closure. No visible risks were observed except for the delay in uploading the contract and payment for a few activities.

Also, it was observed that many activities were cancelled after they were planned. Post- procurement review was conducted, and no serious procurement issues or gaps were found. It was obvious that the project kept its procurement specialists throughout the project life, and this continuity helped the procurement implementation. C. BANK PERFORMANCE Quality at Entry 64. The project design was anchored on the World Bank’s experience and relationship with the GOL since 2005. The World Bank team provided advice on the choice of the contract type, risk allocation measures, and institutional strengthening based on a lot of factors, including lessons learned on OPRC, prevailing post-war condition of infrastructure, low capacity of government and institutions to maintain road infrastructure, and lack of attractiveness of Liberia’s business Page 16 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT environment to the private sector at the time. The project design galvanized resources from donors under the LRTF and from IDA credit to provide lasting infrastructure at less risk to government and more attractive conditions for private sector participation as CEs or MCs. 65. The project design should have been scoped to available funds. The macroeconomic condition in Liberia did not support its ability to co-finance the project in 2011, during the project appraisal.

Even though some economic stability was observed resulting in the completion of the HIPC program in 2010, as at 2009 and during the project preparation, the global financial crisis had affected Liberia’s economy resulting in GDP values dropping from a growth of 7.1 percent in 2008 to 4.9 percent (estimated) in 2009. The GOL’s ability to co-finance was not likely especially since at the time, IDA financing was being sourced for RAP implementation for the URIRP.20 These prevailing conditions should have informed the design of the project to be based on available funds to avoid cancellation of the road maintenance activities. Quality of Supervision 66. The World Bank team successfully provided adequate guidance on contract management and performance monitoring to the IIU staff and the sector. Task teams provided intensive handholding support to augment the institutional arrangement. Twenty-four intensive missions were undertaken, which included the right skill mix to provide the necessary guidance to IIU staff and its management. In addition, the World Bank team provided enhanced interactions including video conferences and monthly review meetings with the IIU. Beside these, technical missions by specialized teams were undertaken to provide guidance on pertinent issues on E&S and gender-based violence/sexual exploitation and abuse.

The World Bank proactively supported the government in the one-year extension of the LRTF closing date to avoid losing US$4.84 million, secured US$90 million AF under IDA credit, and supported the restructuring of the project to achieve the project objectives. 67. Some decisions during implementation bore inherent risks. Even though the team supported the project management effectively, in the absence of counterpart funding, the decision to rehabilitate the 6.1 km urban road because of challenges with human congestion at the Redlight Junction and ELWA intersection under Subcomponents 1.2 and 1.3 was debatable given the extent of social issues involving petty traders in a context where the project was not supposed to finance RAP. The urban section also had no maintenance component which was not consistent with the project’s OPRC direction. Dropping the urban road subcomponents was among the three options of the World Bank to the GOL during the mid-term review to inform subsequent restructuring. The funds used for the intersection and urban section could have financed the entire PM and some RM. The 20-year road life would potentially have been safeguarded and the non- compliances issues related to the petty traders which is still not fully resolved to date would have potentially been avoided. 68.

The team was proactive in ensuring continual engagement on road asset management and institutional strengthening through the design of SECRAMP.21 Under Component 2 of SECRAMP, the MPW and Ministry of Transport will continue the implementation of the road safety action plan designed under LIBRAMP. Also, under Component 3, TA and capacity-building support for transformation of the IIU into a full-fledged road agency is being continued. This arrangement was in anticipation of the government’s inability to undertake the IIU reformation into a road authority capable of taking strategic decisions on road maintenance before the LIBRAMP closing date. AF2 under URIRP made provision for RAP compensation for both URIRP and LIBRAMP. 21 SECRAMP was approved in 2018 and will close in 2027. One part of its PDO is to improve institutional capacity to manage the road sector. Page 17 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT D. RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME 70. The risk to sustainability of the development objective is high. 71. The road asset is at risk of potential deterioration due to lack of maintenance.

The project closed with incomplete maintenance works due to lack of counterpart funding. Liberia’s road asset is valued at 73 percent of GDP22 indicating that the investment required for rehabilitation, upgrade, and maintenance exceeds governments resources. The government financing for maintenance is not reliable especially as commitments made to the CEs at annex 7 have not been paid to date. This puts the Monrovia-Guinea border road at risk of losing its current good condition rating. Early deterioration and reduced safety along the road are expected in the absence of RM and PM. 72. Lack of axle weighing stations along the road corridor exposes the road to early defects and deterioration. In view of the project duration, the project recommended the installation of an axle weighing station by the CE to check overloading to substantiate compensation claims on account of deteriorations due to overloading. This was not built either by the government as a road preservation measure or the CE. The absence of weighing stations along the road corridor exposes the road to uncontrolled overloading and early deterioration of sections as observed from the pavement assessment report. Already 33 km and 17 km are observed to have some defects and are recommended to be corrected and overlain with asphalt. 73. Further institutional reform is necessary to ensure sustainability of the road asset.

The creation of the road maintenance fund, transformation of the IIU into a road authority, and streamlining of the MPW as a policy and maintenance planning entity are all enshrined in the reformation. Whilst the road maintenance fund was created, reforms at the IIU and MPW are pending and necessary to provide a more organized and regulated sector to concretize the trust and support of donor and bilateral groups. Investment through capacity building and TAs have already been made in the road sector to undertake efficient asset management and strategic investments. The autonomy of the IIU as an authority will enhance its ability to make decisions and potentially limit the government’s interference. It is hoped that the continuation of the reformation process under SECRAMP will see the finalization of the institutional reform. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 74. The OPRC was a useful road contract approach to provide continuous preservation of the road asset and institutions in Liberia over 10 years. For a similar country context of having experienced long civil wars and major road infrastructure and institutional capacity losses, the use of a long-term OPRC of ten years provided benefits in institutional capacity development on contract and project management as well as on road asset management practices.

The ten-year OPRC provided the space for uninterrupted maintenance of the road asset after rehabilitation as compared to the traditional method and can be fully implemented to all RM and PM provided there are (a) dedicated funds for all activities, (b) well-structured contracts to ensure conformance by all parties, (c) training of contractors on OPRC, and (d) adequate and well-designed projects. 75. Where ten-year models are not feasible, a shorter duration OPRC could be equally beneficial as an asset management contract tool in countries like Liberia. The ten-year OPRC has the potential to expose contracts to risk related to institutional inadequacies, price fluctuations, and contingencies. In view of this, a shorter duration for OPRC planned for rehabilitation and RM could be suitable. In this way, PM can feasibly be part of the project design 22The road asset value (RSV) was based on the available data on replacement/reconstruction value of the road network as recorded in the RSDP Report, 2023 Page 18 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT recommendations rather than an actual output of the project to avoid or reduce the extent of damages allocated to clients and the government when they are not realized due to inadequate funds as observed in VOs 4 and 1 in annex 7. 76. The payment model for the OPRC was suitable for the long-term project and Liberia’s context in keeping the CEs at post.

Some parts of the rehabilitation lump sum payments were extended into the maintenance payments . The challenges related to force majeure and nonpayment of maintenance work could potentially have disincentivized the CEs from undertaking the maintenance works for six years. Rehabilitation payments were completed per the model in 2022 for both Lots 1 and 2 at which year the CEs suspended the RM. The payment model however was not supported by HDM- 4 for economic analysis. As the OPRC remains useful, revision in HDM-4 should factor the various models to make economic analysis easier. 77. In view of the lack of counterpart financing, which was a major drawback on implementation in Liberia, future operations should ensure that counterpart funds are available before their inclusion in the financing matrix. The situation also exposes the need for government to expand the revenue base for the NRF for maintenance to include other sources like tolling and axle load control which are absent in Liberia. Axle load control besides providing revenue, reduces road deterioration from overloading. The adoption of the RSDP, both for institutional strengthening and streamlining of government investment by allocating available road sector funding according to evidence-based planning is hence crucial. The plan encourages the scoping of projects based on available funds and exploration of other funding options from the private sector to support government budgets on maintenance.

The plan also highlights the significant role of donors in addressing development issues and LIBRAMP provides a good example of this role. The project’s achievements shows that meaningful results can be achieved at scale when partners combine resources to collectively address development challenges. LIBRAMP was realized through funding from IDA and multiple donors under the LRTF. 78. For better data collection and collation and assessment of projects, especially those that are performance- oriented and have longer tenure like the OPRC, the nomination or hiring of an M&E specialist is necessary and their enforcement in the legal covenant is recommended. The specialist would support the update, review, and provide recommendations for adjustment to indicators over the long term. The M&E specialist will also support the monitoring of project performance to enhance delivery of projects. 79. The forceful eviction of the petty traders by the Liberian government highlights a lack of widespread awareness of Bank Policy and Procedures on social and environmental issues, particularly among government officials and establishments. It is therefore important for projects to encourage regular and continuous education and engagements with stakeholders, especially decision-making officials and leaders in government to ensure that both new and existing officials remain informed and up-to-date with current Bank procedures.

EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS I. Introduction 1. This annex documents the economic evaluation of LIBRAMP. The analysis used the CBA approach and quantified the construction costs, RM, and PM of the rehabilitation of the 249 km corridor, and the benefit analysis of lower VOC, passenger time savings, and lower accidents.

These were based on (a) traffic volume, (b) estimated travel cost, (c) investment and maintenance cost, and (d) IRI values. The annex also briefly summarizes the non-quantified economic and social benefits including sustainable job creation resulting from the ten-year OPRC; efficiency gains and administrative cost savings for the government (IIU); and a potential to foster restructuring and performance improvement within the road sector. However, due to the complexity of attribution and limitation of the information, these benefits were not quantified. 2. At ex ante analysis was conducted using the HDM-4 model for Lot 1 and the RED model for Lot 2, assuming a design life of 20 years, with 2010 as the base year. The appraisal of Lot 1 urban section - Coca Cola to ELWA junction was done in 2017 following the scale up and did not include maintenance. The project was expected to generate an NPV of US$48.8 million and an EIRR of 23 percent for Lot 1 rural (Monrovia Red Light-Gbarnga), an EIRR of 17.3 percent and NPV of $5.97 million for Lot 1 urban (Coca Cola to ELWA junction), and an NPV of US$9.2 million and EIRR of 18 percent for Lot 2 (Gbarnga-Ganta-Guinea border). 3. The ex post economic evaluation utilized the HDM-4 model for both lots, as RED is deemed inappropriate for the evaluation of the paved road.

According to the Africa Transport Technical Note (1999), road deterioration equations, such as those in the HDM models, which account for road roughness over time, based on condition, traffic, and maintenance characteristics, are not implemented in RED. Instead, RED uses the concept of average service levels, which is suitable for low-volume unpaved roads. RED assumes a constant average level of service for both with- and without-project cases over the 20-year analysis period, which is considered inappropriate. The ICR analysis therefore used vehicle characteristics, utilization data, travel time costs, and climate information derived from the previous RED analysis but adjusted as necessary in HDM-4. 4. Both the appraisal and ex post analysis included construction costs, RM, and PM. The PM cost and cost of RM from 2022 are assumed and not actual costs during the project implementation tenure. Construction and RM cost up to 2022 were based on actual construction and RM expenses. Calibration was performed at Level 1 with default values, as was done during the appraisal phase. Vehicle fleet data, traffic projections, and road pavement data were sourced from the initial appraisal documents and pavement evaluation reports completed at the end of construction. II. Economic Analysis for Lot 1 Rural Section (Coca Cola to Gbarnga) and Urban Section (Coca Cola to ELWA junction) 5.

The planning horizon for the project ex post analysis was set at 20 years, with 2012 as the base year for the rural section and 2019 for the urban section. 6. Rural section. The project case scenario considered the actual costs incurred to date, amounting to US$156.92 million for construction and RM and estimated cost for PM and post-closure RM. This scenario resulted in an EIRR of 21.9 percent and an NPV of US$73.87 million, indicating a favorable economic outcome. 7. Urban section. This section did not align with the OPRC contract methodology as it included only construction of the urban road and ELWA roundabout whose cost totaled US$20.05 million, yielding an EIRR of 14.9 percent and an NPV of US$3.19 million, demonstrating economic viability, although lower than anticipated at appraisal. Page 30 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT III. Economic Analysis for Lot 2 - Gbarnga to Guinea Border Section 8. The analysis considered the actual costs paid up to March 2024, totaling $56.21 million for construction, RM, contingencies, emergency works as well as estimated cost for RM and PM during the 20-year project life. This scenario demonstrated economic viability, with an EIRR of 19.1 percent and an NPV of US$20.33 million. Additionally, the roadway length increased slightly and the cost per kilometer increased significantly compared to appraisal.

Although there are outstanding claims, the EIRR remained close, but the NPV was lower than anticipated. IV. Comparison of Project and Appraisal Economic Analysis 9. Several factors may account for the drop in the project appraisal NPV and EIRR at completion. These include variations in project road lengths at appraisal versus completion, differences in the projected cost per kilometer at appraisal, and the potential overestimation of benefits during appraisal. (a) Methodology. Appraisal analysis used the RED model for the Lot 2 economic assessment due to the deteriorated road condition (IRI = 12 m/km) at the time, with largely gravel or unpaved surfaces. In addition, there was insufficient data for the detailed analysis and deterioration modeling required by HDM-4. Therefore, the RED model was used. The ICR analysis, however, uses the more appropriate HDM-4 model for both lots. (b) Base year. The appraisal evaluation used a 20-year period starting in 2010, based on 2009 traffic data and VOC. However, the actual contract commenced in 2012 for Lot 1 rural and 2013 for Lot 2, considering the tender and procurement processes. Therefore, the ICR evaluation utilized a 2012 base year for Lot 1 rural, with 2012 VOC and utilization data and actual 2010 traffic data, and a 2013 base year for Lot 2, using 2013 VOC and 2012 traffic data. This provided the most up-to-date CBA. (c) Rehabilitation cost and payments.

For Lot 1 rural, the rehabilitation cost estimated during appraisal was US$96.4 million, while the actual project cost amounted to US$156.92 million, nearly double the estimated cost. On a per-kilometer basis, the costs were US$534,486 pre-construction and US$888,209 post- construction. Although appraisal estimated a construction period of three years, the actual construction took five years. However, payments were distributed over ten years as per the OPRC project design. For Lot 2, the appraisal estimated the rehabilitation cost at US$479,522 per kilometer, while the actual cost was also nearly double at US$801,397 per kilometer with a two-year construction period. However, the actual construction took three years, with payments spread over ten years according to the OPRC project design. (d) RM cost. This was estimated at US$6.8 million per year, compared to the actual cost of US$344,00 per year for Lot 1 rural, and US$2.1 million per year, compared to the actual cost of US$136,000 per year for Lot 2. The estimated cost was over ten times higher than the actual cost in the OPRC. At project closure, the constructed road was yet to receive its first 33 km of overlay, with an average IRI of less than 3 m/km, whereas the appraisal analysis planned for overlays in years eight and sixteen of the 20-year analysis period. (e) Traffic Volume (ADT). In 2009, Lot 1 rural had an ADT of 2,451 vehicles.

The projected growth rates were 35 percent from 2019–2012, 10 percent from 2012–2013, and 5 percent per year thereafter, leading to a cumulative ADT of 195,514 vehicles. However, the ex post cumulative traffic was assessed at 93,579 vehicles, indicating significantly lower demand anticipated. For Lot 2, ADT in 2009 was 1,473 vehicles with estimated growth rates of 35 percent from 2009–2012 and 10 percent from 2012–2013 resulting in an ADT of 4,385 vehicles, marking a 300 percent increase over five years. In contrast, the ex-post traffic volumes increased from an ADT of 1,540 vehicles to 2,520 vehicles over five years, marking a 164 percent increase from 2013– 2017. The cumulative ADT for the ex-post evaluation is assessed at 117,497 vehicles, compared to 71,587 Page 31 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT vehicles for the appraisal period, also significantly lower demand than anticipated. Despite the low traffic volume on both lots, overloading is suspected to be the cause of deterioration at some sections along the roadway. No recent traffic volume count data has been collected for the project road. 10. The project's viability at completion remains attractive, even though the cost per kilometer is higher for both lots. The economic analysis also indicates that the projected GHG emissions have been reduced from the projected 111,420 tons of CO2 per year at appraisal to 53,148.90 tons of CO2 per year. V. Conclusion 11.

In conclusion, the economic analysis for both Lot 1 and Lot 2 demonstrates economic viability under the project case scenarios, with EIRRs indicating higher returns than the planning discount rate of 12 percent. Overall, the project remains resilient to potential cost escalations, ensuring long-term sustainability and validating the investment in these infrastructure initiatives. Page 32 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT ANNEX 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS 1. The GOL has reviewed the findings of the World Bank’s ICR, and their comments have been addressed. The Borrower’s ICR has been submitted to the project team and is pending filing for information and referencing in WBDocs. The Borrower’s ICR is summarized below. 2. World Bank Performance. Throughout project implementation, seasoned World Bank professionals led task teams, bringing expertise in infrastructure, FM, procurement, and safeguards. Their diverse skills ensured tailored supervision and support, enabling necessary adjustments and restructurings to address challenges. Regular support from technical and fiduciary teams maximized the project's impact, with key decisions documented in Aide-Memoires. The World Bank's proactive oversight, timely 'no objections’, and expedited fund disbursements kept the project on track.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Despite challenges like high turnover of task team leaders affecting continuity, Monrovia-based World Bank staff provided continuous support, ensuring compliance and contributing significantly to the project's success. Overall, the implementation support and guidance provided by the World Bank were considered satisfactory, significantly contributing to the project's progress and success. 3. PDO achievement and key project impact factors. At project closing, all PDO outcome indicators met or exceeded targets, but intermediate results indicators had mixed results due to activity cancellations due to financial constraints and weak enforcement of zonal laws. The achievement of the project results was a result of (a) the OPRC contract approach which brought substantial efficiencies in contracting; it facilitated the completion of the Suakoko Highway rehabilitation and maintenance phase efficiently, (b) sectoral strengthening contributing to experience development and creating employment opportunities which presents broader socioeconomic benefits beyond infrastructure development, and (c) effective coordination among stakeholders, including government agencies, donors, and local communities, essential for aligning efforts and resources toward project objectives.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Collaboration between the MPW, local authorities, and community leaders facilitated smoother implementation and improved project outcomes, and the flexible management of the project allowed for adjustments to be made in response to changing circumstances. 4. Beside these key positive factors that contributed to the PDO achievement and project completion, issues such as (a) counterpart financing shortfall, (b) exchange rate fluctuations and cost escalation, (c) road safety and encroachment risks, (d) logistical transportation challenges resulting in difficulty in transporting construction materials and equipment to remote project sites posing logistical challenges, (e) nonpayment of government commitment, (f) funding delays from the GOL, (g) site handover delays, (h) impact of EVD and COVID-19 pandemics, (i) lack of coordination among utility agencies, waste management, and the MPW, and (j) challenges with petty traders and RoW and the subsequent noncompliance issues affected the project negatively. 5. Lessons learned. In summary, the LIBRAMP was hampered by financial, administrative, and coordination challenges. Nonpayment of government commitments, delays in fund releases, health crises, insufficient resources, and coordination issues all contributed to significant project delays and increased costs.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: The project offered key lessons relevant to both the country and the region, including the following: • Government should ensure that future projects make provision for contingencies, including compensation for RAP and PAP funding commitments in loan agreements to prevent delays. • Local government involvement and enforcement of regulations are crucial for smooth project implementation. Page 33 The World Bank Liberia Road Asset Management Project - LIBRAMP (P125574) ICR DOCUMENT • Detailed Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidelines for quarry mining and borrow pit exploitation are necessary for effective monitoring. • Investment in tools and procedures aligned with ECOWAS standards is essential for maintaining road quality. • Strengthening the Liberia National Road Fund and setting up a road agency is critical for effective road maintenance. • Prioritizing and operationalizing the road asset management system ensures efficient fund allocation. • Improved processes of fund flow from the LRA to the NRF will enhance predictable cashflow to that entity • New World Bank policies should be clearly defined and managed proactively to avoid delays and compliance issues. • Managing project commitments and ensuring timely payments can reduce excessive contractor claims and costs. • Measurable indicators for road safety activities other than training are necessary for effective implementation and monitoring.
